headlines.article_text: Rene Haas to remain CEO of chipmaker Arm through 2033 amid Nvidia top job chatter Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu In this article USDAUD= ARM NVDA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Rene Haas, chief executive officer of Arm Holdings Plc, speaks during the Arm Everywhere event in San Francisco, California, US, on Tuesday, March 24, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas has extended his contract to lead the chip designer through 2033, confirming his leadership role at the company amid speculation that Nvidia could tap him for the top job after Jensen Huang's resignation. Haas was among several names floated as potential candidates to replace Huang, who resigned as Nvidia's CEO earlier this month following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia's board had approached Haas in its search for a successor to Huang, the Financial Times had reported. Nvidia's finance chief Colette Kress is currently interim CEO at the company. Analysts also pointed to Haas as a solid candidate for the top job at Nvidia, given he spent his formative years at the company — rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business — before joining Arm in 2013. U.S.-listed shares of Arm were up nearly 9% in premarket trading amid a broader lift in AI stocks as they rebounded after a bruising selloff last week. Haas' standing as a high-profile semiconductor industry figure and his familiarity with Nvidia were seen as key reasons making him a good fit for the CEO role at Nvidia. He became the British chipmaker's CEO in 2022 and oversaw its return to public markets through a $65 billion Nasdaq listing the following year. Arm licenses processor designs used across smartphones, PCs, servers and connected devices, and Nvidia relies heavily on the company's chip architecture. "I've never been more confident about Arm's future ... I'm wholly committed to realizing Arm's full potential for many years to come," Haas said in a statement on Monday. Haas will also assume the role of vice chairman of SoftBank Group, effective December 1, Arm said. Arm is majority-owned by SoftBank. Haas is a board member at the Japanese conglomerate and, in April, took over the reins of SoftBank's international business. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal — and application developers beyond — lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," Meredith Whittaker, president of the app's nonprofit parent Signal Foundation, said in a Friday blog post . Signal last year introduced similar restrictions against Microsoft's Recall AI on Windows 11. Its latest move adds to a broader push by companies including United Airlines , JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab to limit or block AI agents over security and for customer-protection concerns. Whittaker said the new protections do not address every way an agent might gain access to data, including by retrieving content already stored on a user's device. Signal also warned that third-party agents such as Meta's Muse could gain access to private app content through permissions granted during setup. "Application-level protections will always have gaps, so the data an agent can reach has to be classified, permissioned and recoverable before the agent arrives," said Tianyi Jiang, CEO of data management and protection software company AvePoint. AvePoint's State of AI 2026 report found that 88.4% of surveyed organizations had experienced at least one AI-agent-related security breach in the previous year. The survey covered 750 IT leaders globally. "We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data," said Whittaker. Restricted entry Banks are also restricting third-party AI agents from accessing customer accounts. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said in October that outside agents were too risky for the bank and its clients. Morgan Stanley has blocked third-party agents from its platforms, Reuters reported. Meanwhile, Charles Schwab CEO Richard Wurster said the brokerage blocks unauthorized agents to protect clients and the firm. Singapore's OCBC Bank has said it will not let third-party agents to interact with the bank to transfer money autonomously and warned that "customers should exercise caution" when using such agents for banking. United Airlines said Nov. 11 that it would restrict unauthorized agents from booking or managing tickets, citing risks that they could expose customer information, make unintended purchases or violate aviation rules. "To book flights or do your grocery shop, an agent needs your email, accounts and payment details," said Mick Maleishko, an AI advocate at identity verification and compliance platform Sumsub. He said that level of access creates a risk of account hijacking because actions taken by an agent may appear to a retailer or bank to have been authorized by the user. Singapore Airlines , by contrast, is an early partner of Meta's Muse. Meta said users can ask the agent to explore travel, ticketing and reservation options through the airline. "People treat agent risk as one-size-fits-all rather than matching the security needed to the actual task," said Yat Siu, executive chairman and co-founder of Animoca Brands. He said agents could help consumers act on their intentions and help businesses reach customers directly, but the risks vary by task. "There's a much higher risk around an agent able to move meaningful sums of money or access sensitive personal data, than one making your restaurant reservations," Siu said. "The reality is that, just like internet applications to date, agents require tiered safeguards." AI adoption grows in Asia, but measuring the gains remains tricky
headlines.summary: Businesses across Asia-Pacific are seeing returns from AI investments, even as confidence in measuring those gains varies, according to an AWS survey.
headlines.article_text: AI adoption grows in Asia, but measuring the gains remains tricky Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Some 58% of businesses using AI said their investments had surpassed initial costs, according to an AWS survey. More businesses are moving AI projects from experimentation into production, AWS executive Jaime Vallés told CNBC. A shortage of AI and digital skills remains a key barrier, cited by 48% of businesses, according to the survey. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT An Amazon Web Services AI data center in New Carlisle, Indiana, on Oct. 2, 2025. Noah Berger | Getty Images Businesses across Asia-Pacific say their investments in artificial intelligence are paying off, with the technology helping boost productivity and revenue. But putting a number on those gains is proving far less straightforward. Some 58% of businesses using AI said their investments had already surpassed their initial costs, yet just 12% were very confident in their ability to accurately measure their return on investment, according to research conducted by Strand Partners for Amazon Web Services . APAC, to make it simpler, has all the ingredients to be in my view the core or the center of worldwide innovation. Jaime Vallés VP, Amazon Web Services The survey included 9,750 business leaders across 10 Asia-Pacific markets: Australia, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. The biggest shift over the past year has been the growing number of companies moving AI projects into production, Jaime Vallés, AWS vice president for Asia Pacific, Japan and China, told CNBC in an exclusive interview. "From year over year, probably the biggest difference is you're seeing a lot of ideas put into production," Vallés said. From pilots to results Despite the reported financial benefits, many businesses remain in the early stages of AI adoption. The survey found that 64% of businesses using AI across Asia-Pacific and Japan still rely on general-purpose AI tools or ready-made solutions for specific tasks, while only 19% of businesses have a formal and comprehensive AI strategy. Among those with such an AI strategy, 35% had reached the most advanced stage of adoption, compared with just 8% of businesses without one, according to the research. Technology alone is not enough to turn AI investments into meaningful business outcomes, Vallés said. He pointed to what he called the "four Rs of readiness": technological, cultural, skills and personal readiness. "Where we see more meaningful impact is when you see the leadership using AI, building a culture of using AI and using AI to transform and not automate," Vallés said. Financial services is among the sectors seeing stronger AI adoption. Vallés pointed to Vietnam's Techcombank as an example, saying the bank is using AI to assess loan applications and expand access to credit for small businesses. The technology has helped the bank to analyze more data and approve some loan applications that might otherwise have been rejected, he said. Techcombank, one of Vietnam's largest commercial banks, serves more than 16.5 million retail and corporate customers. According to an AWS case study , its modernization of digital banking infrastructure using AWS improved application response times by up to 35% and cut the time needed to launch new product features by 30%. What's next for Asia? AI adoption continued to expand across Asia-Pacific, with all 10 markets surveyed recording increases from the previous year. Australia led the group with an adoption rate of 61%, followed by Singapore at 59% and South Korea at 58%. Still, businesses face significant obstacles to scaling AI investments. A shortage of AI and digital skills remains a key barrier, cited by 48% of respondents as an obstacle to adoption or expansion. Despite those challenges, Vallés expressed optimism about Asia-Pacific's role in AI innovation, pointing to the region's cultural diversity and range of perspectives. "I am convinced that most of the innovation in the fullness of time will come from our region," he said. Vallés added that Asia-Pacific has the ingredients to become a global center for innovation, citing its diversity, talent, startup ecosystem and technology. "APAC, to make it simpler, has all the ingredients to be in my view the core or the center of worldwide innovation," he said. Governments across Asia also play a role in supporting Al adoption and addressing barriers to its wider use. About 72% of government respondents said Al had increased productivity, according to a report released by the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council in November, which surveyed more than 500 experts across 23 Asia-Pacific economies. Around 59% of respondents viewed government support as a moderately or very important factor in accelerating AI adoption next year, though existing regulations were also seen as a constraint, the report showed. Such support is also taking share through regional cooperation. The Asian Development Bank and South Korea established a $20 million fund to help developing economies adopt Al and address gaps in digital skills and infrastructure, according to an announcement by the bank earlier this month.
